title: Boundaries & Difficult Conversations
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: Something a person would like, without assuming someone else must provide it.
glossary.example: I would prefer to finish work calls before dinner.
glossary.limit: A preference may be important, but naming it does not create an obligation for someone else.

glossary.definition: An invitation for another person to do something, which they may accept or refuse.
glossary.example: Could you send non-urgent reports before six?
glossary.limit: A request becomes different when refusal is met with retaliation or threatened punishment.

glossary.definition: A limit on what somebody will participate in or how they will respond.
glossary.example: I won't answer routine work calls outside the hours I have agreed to work.
glossary.limit: A boundary concerns your own participation; it is not a licence to govern another adult's choices.

glossary.definition: An attempt to determine another person's behaviour through rules or leverage they have not agreed to.
glossary.example: You are not allowed to speak with that friend, or I will make you pay for it.
glossary.limit: Power, safety and the practical consequences matter more than whether someone calls the rule a boundary.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
We can tell people what we want, ask them to change something and decide what we will do ourselves. Those are different actions, and confusing them causes many arguments.

Which parts of an agreement can one person decide for themselves?
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: What preference means
nodes.body:
Something a person would like, without assuming someone else must provide it.

For example: I would prefer to finish work calls before dinner.

One important limit: A preference may be important, but naming it does not create an obligation for someone else.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: I would prefer to finish work calls before dinner. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports preference. Something a person would like, without assuming someone else must provide it. A preference may be important, but naming it does not create an obligation for someone else.
nodes.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: What personal boundary means
nodes.body:
A limit on what somebody will participate in or how they will respond.

For example: I won't answer routine work calls outside the hours I have agreed to work.

One important limit: A boundary concerns your own participation; it is not a licence to govern another adult's choices.

nodes.title: What control means
nodes.body:
An attempt to determine another person's behaviour through rules or leverage they have not agreed to.

For example: You are not allowed to speak with that friend, or I will make you pay for it.

One important limit: Power, safety and the practical consequences matter more than whether someone calls the rule a boundary.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Rae dislikes receiving work calls after 7 pm. Kit is a colleague whose project sometimes runs late.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.
nodes.scenario: Rae dislikes receiving work calls after 7 pm. Kit is a colleague whose project sometimes runs late.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Could you stop calling me after seven?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sometimes the reports don't come through until eight.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I need my evenings to be uninterrupted.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I can't promise never to call if something urgent happens.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
checks.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

items.label: “Could you stop calling me after seven?”
Rae names a limit on her own availability and proposes a way to meet legitimate work needs. This differs from prescribing what another adult is allowed to do.
“Sometimes the reports don't come through until eight.”
Kit may face genuine operational duties that require a different rota or on-call arrangement rather than an informal promise.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:

Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Rae names a limit on her own availability and proposes a way to meet legitimate work needs. This differs from prescribing what another adult is allowed to do.

Another possibility: Kit may face genuine operational duties that require a different rota or on-call arrangement rather than an informal promise.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Clarify the actual job requirements and separate emergencies from preferences for immediate replies. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Clarify the actual job requirements and separate emergencies from preferences for immediate replies.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: A manager confirms that there is no after-hours on-call requirement and the reports can be handled the next working day.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The operational necessity explanation weakens. Rae's proposed communication limit becomes easier to implement without risking service continuity.
nodes.counterexample: Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.
nodes.sources: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Manual, interpersonal effectiveness; occupational boundary research.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

lessons.title: A boundary isn't a command
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of preferences, requests and boundaries.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual (2015), interpersonal effectiveness.
nodes.scenario: Ellie and Dev share a flat. Dev occasionally invites guests without warning.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I need notice before people come into our shared space.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I don't want to ask permission every time I see my friends.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm asking for notice, not to choose your friends.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What if plans happen at the last minute?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'll use my room if I need quiet, but we should agree how shared spaces work.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That sounds different from deciding who I'm allowed to invite.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Dev thinks providing notice amounts to requesting permission for every visitor.
Ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself.
Ellie wants to control which friends Dev may see.
A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
options.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

options.label: Ellie may be reacting to a prior uncomfortable visit and now anticipating the same problem with other guests.
options.feedback: Past experience might explain the importance of notice, though it has not been described in the current exchange.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself. Ellie wants to control which friends Dev may see. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.

checks.prompt: You are Ellie. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Ask each person to set out their own immediate concern before deciding whether to escalate.
options.reply: I want enough notice to decide whether to use our living room.
options.consequence: This can reveal different priorities, but it may also delay an urgent factual correction.
options.feedback: This can reveal different priorities, but it may also delay an urgent factual correction.

options.label: Could we agree on advance notice for overnight guests first, then discuss shorter visits separately?
options.reply: I want enough notice to decide whether to use our living room.
options.consequence: A narrower agreement may be easier to implement but could leave the general notice concern unresolved.
options.feedback: A narrower agreement may be easier to implement but could leave the general notice concern unresolved.

options.label: I'd like a message before someone arrives; I don't need to approve whom you invite.
options.reply: I want enough notice to decide whether to use our living room.
options.consequence: This clearly distinguishes notice from permission, though they still need a workable last-minute arrangement.
options.feedback: This clearly distinguishes notice from permission, though they still need a workable last-minute arrangement.

options.label: Can we agree on a message before guests arrive, including how to handle last-minute visits?
options.reply: Yes. We can discuss exceptions when they happen.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Can we trial a shared calendar for visits and review whether it gives us enough notice?
options.feedback: A practical system could help, but it is only useful if both flatmates agree to use it.

nodes.title: If the first response fails
nodes.prompt: The other person rejects a reasonable direct request and the practical concern is unresolved. What next?
nodes.conceptId: boundaries-module-01:Assertiveness, behavioural boundaries and shared problem-solving
nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

nodes.explanation: A sound response is judged by what it makes possible, not by whether it can instantly change somebody else. I won't respond to routine calls after seven. Could we agree a separate route for a genuine emergency?

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.conceptId: boundaries-module-01:Assertiveness, behavioural boundaries and shared problem-solving
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Clarify the actual job requirements and separate emergencies from preferences for immediate replies.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Clarify the actual job requirements and separate emergencies from preferences for immediate replies.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

options.label: Compare the accounts against records made at the time rather than relying on recollection alone.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A partner says, 'My boundary is that you're not allowed to talk to any of your old friends.' The other partner wants to distinguish a request from control.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Rae names a limit on her own availability and proposes a way to meet legitimate work needs. This differs from prescribing what another adult is allowed to do.

Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.

glossary.definition: Something a person would like, without assuming someone else must provide it.
glossary.example: I would prefer to finish work calls before dinner.
glossary.limit: A preference may be important, but naming it does not create an obligation for someone else.

glossary.definition: An invitation for another person to do something, which they may accept or refuse.
glossary.example: Could you send non-urgent reports before six?
glossary.limit: A request becomes different when refusal is met with retaliation or threatened punishment.

glossary.definition: A limit on what somebody will participate in or how they will respond.
glossary.example: I won't answer routine work calls outside the hours I have agreed to work.
glossary.limit: A boundary concerns your own participation; it is not a licence to govern another adult's choices.

glossary.definition: An attempt to determine another person's behaviour through rules or leverage they have not agreed to.
glossary.example: You are not allowed to speak with that friend, or I will make you pay for it.
glossary.limit: Power, safety and the practical consequences matter more than whether someone calls the rule a boundary.
